“Lodha Developers Limited  
Q2 FY 2027 Post Results Conference Call” 
November 2, 2026 
 
 
 
       
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
Management: 
Mr. Abhishek Lodha: Managing Director  
 
 
Mr. Sushil Kumar Modi: Whole-time Director, Group Finance Director 
 
 
 
Mr. Sanjay Chauhan: Chief Financial Officer    
                                      
                                       Mr. Rajendra Joshi – Regional Chief Executive Officer, Bangalore 
 
 
Mr. Anand Kumar: Head of Investor Relations  
 
Mr. Chintan Parikh:  Co-Head of Investor Relations  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
2 
 
Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to the Lodha Developers Limited Q2 FY27 
Analyst Conference Call. As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and 
there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions after the presentation concludes. Should 
you need assistance during this conference call, please signal an operator by pressing star then 
zero on your touchtone phone. Please note that this conference has been recorded. I now hand 
the conference over to Mr. Chintan Parikh from Lodha Developers Limited. Thank you, and over 
to you, sir. 
Chintan Parikh: 
Thank you, Swapnali. Welcome to Lodha Developers Q2 FY27 Conference Call. Today, we have 
with us Mr. Abhishek Lodha, Managing Director; Mr. Sushil Kumar Modi, Group Finance 
Director; Mr. Sanjay Chauhan, Chief Financial Officer; Mr. Rajendra Joshi, CEO of Bangalore. I 
would now like to invite Abhishek to make his opening remarks. Over to you, Abhishek. 
Abhishek Lodha: 
Thank you, Chintan. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Wishing all of you 
and your families a very Happy Diwali and a prosperous new year. The first half of fiscal '27 has 
been the strongest in Lodha's history. We've delivered profit after tax of INR 2,386 crores, 
which is up 63%. 
 
Our revenue at INR 9,460 crores is up 30%. Our pre-sales of INR 96 billion are up by 7%; all 3 
being the highest ever in our history. We have achieved this while moderately reducing our net 
debt, which now stands at about INR 52 billion, about 0.2x equity. As we had told you at the 
start of the year, our H1 pre-sales would be about 40% to 42% in the first half and the balance 
in the second half.  
This came in at about 40.3%. The numbers for the second half of the year are likely to be coming 
with a mix of about INR 6000 crores to INR 7,000 crores of development company pre-sales in 
both Q3 as well as Q4 and 1 data center land transaction of about INR 1,500 crores in the fourth 
quarter for the full year number at about INR 24,000 crores of pre-sales. 
 
Having said that, we expect to easily beat our profit guidance of 20% growth which would have 
taken us to just over INR 4,000 crores. And in the first half, having already touched INR 2,400 
crores, we feel very confident of being able to beat this guidance quite comfortably. Over the 
medium term, we believe that the underlying profitability of the business is getting better. 
And therefore, will support an improvement in our return on equity further and will also aid 
our DevCo to become net debt-free over the next 2 to 3 years, which is in line with our previous 
guidance. In terms of where we stand now, at the start of the second half, we've had a strong 
start to the third quarter. October, the festive season has been strong. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
3 
 
 
We expect that the momentum in the market will continue through this year, and this is in 
spite of the fact that the adverse effects, if any, of the rising interest rates have already started. 
Having said that, we believe that the segments that we serve are not really affected by the 
change in interest rates, and hence, we feel that there will be no adverse effect of any 
moderate further increase in interest rates from this point onwards. 
 
I would like to highlight in terms of our Q2 performance that our new launch in Bangalore 
delivered significant success and therefore, Bangalore's pre-sales for the second quarter was 
over INR 1,800 crores. This tells you about the significance of the fact that we've delivered INR 
96 billion of sales in the first half with only INR 4,000 crores of GDV of new launches.  
In the second half of the year, we have a further almost just under INR 20,000 crores of new 
launches planned. And while 1 or 2 launches may move by a month or 2, overall, the program 
is a very solid and dispersed across different geographies, which will enable us to deliver on 
our guidance for the year. 
 
I would also like to update you that we just entered and have started the pre-sales for our first 
project in Gurugram NCR and the start has been quite constructive; We believe that this will 
be the start of the for city, which will over time contribute to our growth and our profitability.  
In terms of other updates, the Mulund-Airoli-Palava Freeway is now clinically complete. And 
we think that it will open in the next few weeks. And with that, Airoli will be just 20 minutes 
from Palava and Mulund will be only a 25-minute travel from Palava. Both of these will make a 
big difference to allow our attractiveness. 
 
We expect that calendar year 2027 will lead to a significant uptick in pre-sales at Palava on 
account of this infrastructure improvement. Obviously, the opening of the bullet train, which 
is scheduled for 2029, will be a significant step further in the direction of Palava moving from 
a secondary suburb to becoming a primary suburb. 
 
In terms of our collections and cash flows. The first half collections were at about INR 76 billion, 
up 19% year-on-year, and the operating cash flow was about INR 27 billion. Q2 collections were 
about INR 35 billion following the usual pattern, whereas the Q1 collections obviously had the 
land transaction as a part of it and hence, were higher. 
 
In the second half, we expect that our operating cash flow as it was in last fiscal, will significantly 
crank up, and we expect full year that our operating cash flow will be put around INR 85 billion 
or thereabouts. In terms of our data center platform, we are seeing good progress both in the 
land demand as well as in the BTS boxes.  
 
 

 
 
 
4 
 
We expect to have the definitive documents executed for the first BTS box of in this fiscal year 
and to start construction for the boxes also in this fiscal year with a view to delivering those 
boxes to the end tenant in fiscal '29, and therefore, starting the rental earnings from our data 
center BTS program in fiscal '29 itself. 
 
In addition to this, we expect the land sales to be an ongoing and continuous and predictable 
pattern with 1 transaction happening every 6 months or thereabout. And this will lead to a 
significant not only cash flow but also positive impact on profitability.  
Speaking of profitability, I would like to point out that the numbers that you see for Q2 are 
really the underlying profitability of our solid development business because there were no 
land sales in this quarter. Both the embedded EBITDA as well as the PAT are a real reflection 
of the strength of profitability of the business, driven by the strength of our brand.  
In terms of the industry, there are a few questions which often come up, and I would like to 
share our views about these. The first 1 is the war in the Middle East and how it is affecting 
housing demand. In our opinion, the direct demand effect is limited to the NRI demand from 
the Gulf which is about 4% to 5% of the sales. The broader effects due to the effective 
management of the fuel availability as well as prices by the government have been largely 
absorbed and that is reflected in India's June quarter GDP growth at about 7.8% and 
industrial production growing by over 6.7% in September. 
 
We are hopeful that as and when the Middle East situation stabilizes, there will be a positive 
momentum to Indian growth with oil prices coming down and as a consequence, is being 
supportive of both the Indian rupee as well as domestic growth.  
                                                    In terms of the 25 basis points increase in the repo rate by the RBI in October. We would like to 
point out that about 50% of our sales by value come in the segment between INR 1 crores to 
INR 5 crores value of the unit and the balance comes from the segment above INR 5 crores. 
Impact of mortgages on the segment above INR 5 crores is negligible. And hence, we do not 
expect any impact of interest rate increases in that segment. 
 
In the segment between INR 1 crores to INR 5 crores, we see an average LTV of high 40s, low 
50s. And while there will be some moderate impact of the increase in interest rates on this 
segment, we see no change in our outlook which is really driven by the significant gap in high-
quality supply in the marketplace.  
The related point I would like to speak about is that is there an oversupply building up? And 
whether there is a likelihood of that impacting the market going forward? We've been speaking 
about the redevelopment phenomena in Mumbai for 3 years now. And as you can notice, us 
as well as other large developers continue to scale up their pre-sales.  
 

 
 
 
5 
 
This really is a reflection of the fact that the market is getting increasingly tuned towards large 
organized and branded developers. And the supply from these Grade A+ and Grade A 
developers is seen and dealt with by the market in a very different manner from the rest of the 
supply. 
 
India, in the first 9 months of 2026 has seen about 60 million square feet of office absorption 
with about 40% of it by the global capability centers. We also see that AI is reorganizing 
workflows, but we also see that it is not all negative for India and on the contrary, as we saw 
in the example of PwC where PwC U.S. and PwC India have come together to set up a large-
scale consulting venture to serve U.S. clients in India. 
We believe that AI given the high level of technology and the high level of need for execution, 
implementation support will be a positive for Indian jobs and therefore, as by extension in 
housing. Our performance in Bangalore in the last quarter is an indication of our belief that for 
the strong brands, the demand continues to remain robust, and there is a significant supply-
demand gap. 
 
I would also like to highlight that Newsweek has again named Lodha amongst the World’s 1,000 
most trustworthy companies, the only Indian real estate company on the list for the second 
year running. We believe that this is a recognition of the way that our business is conducted 
and about how society at large as well as our direct sale stakeholders like employees and 
customers are perceiving our company.  
Through the Lodha Foundation, the Lodha Mathematical Sciences Institute hosted 55 
researchers this quarter with more than 90 from 15 countries expected in the coming 
semester. The team comprising of 6 Students from Lodha Genius Program placed second at the 
Eking 2026 in Switzerland.  
And we continue to support the communities that we work in by direct cash transfers as well 
as health insurance for a large number of families. With this, I would like to hand over and call 
in Mr. Rajendra Joshi, the CEO of our Bangalore business to speak about the Q2 launch that we 
had and what we're seeing on the ground in Bangalore. 
Rajendra Joshi: 
Thank you, sir. Good afternoon to everyone. I will speak in brief about the Bangalore market 
and our journey in Bangalore. The Bangalore residential real estate market is now over      INR 
1 lakh crores as of FY '26, nearly tripling in size over the last 4-to-5-year period, driven by both 
volume and price.  
The market has continued to premiumize with homes priced over INR 2 crores, increasing their 
contribution from 40% in FY '24 to 50% in FY '26 over the last 2 years, while the aggregate 
volume in square feet terms have largely remained steady, premium housing has continued to 
grow. 

 
 
 
6 
 
 
Pricing growth has been healthy at about 10% in most locations during this period with some 
pockets witnessing stronger price growth on account of improving connectivity and new job 
hub creation. Supply continues to be on the healthy side with an average inventory position of 
about 18 months in the last 2 years.  
The market continues to remain robust in FY '27 with the first half of this year, recording an 
absorption of about INR 52,500 crores, up 10% over the same period of last year. Pricing 
momentum continues to be steady as well with an average increase of about 6% compared to 
first half of FY '26. 
 
The INR 2 crores and above segment in which we operate continues to perform strongly, as 
we've mentioned, contributes about 50% of the overall market demand. Demand continues to 
be strong across the key growth corridors of North, East and Southeast Bangalore, supported 
by cities growing base of white-collar professionals across GCC technology companies. 
And the start-up ecosystem with majority of these buyers belonging to mid - to senior 
managers in these organizations. Office absorption being a lead indicator of residential demand 
remains at record levels. Bangalore recorded nearly 17 million square feet of net office 
absorption in calendar year '25, the highest ever for the city.  
This is followed by 8.3 million square feet in first half of this calendar year. GCC is continuing 
to be an important driver of this demand and Bangalore remains a major GCC hub. Global giants 
such as Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan continue to have significant GCC presence in Bangalore, 
and many of these centers have moved beyond just being back-office work locations to 
strategic hub for digital engineering and core product development.  
This, I think, is something that is really driving the recent demand in the Bangalore City. The 
city's Cyber ecosystem is another source of demand, spanning late-stage and well-funded 
early-stage companies. Consumer tech in particular, has boomed over the last 3 to 4 years with 
names such as Swiggy, Razorpay, Meesho, Zepto contributing to a growing uniform base and 
the wave of IPOs.  
Looking ahead, strong job creation, sustained investor confidence in the start-up ecosystem 
and ongoing infrastructure development, such as the upcoming North Bangalore Metro line 
and the Satellite Town Ring Road are expected to be key catalysts for the continued residential 
growth. 
Coming to our journey in Bangalore. We entered Bangalore with the launch of Lodha Mirabelle 
next to Manyata's Business Park in North Bangalore in November. Our first couple of years 
were focused on establishing Lodha as a premium brand in the city, building a strong local 
organization and demonstrating our ability to deliver a differentiated product and a customer 
experience. Having successfully completed this initial phase, we are now firmly in the growth 
phase of our Bangalore journey. 

 
 
 
7 
 
 
From two projects in FY '25 and about INR 700 crores in pre-sales. We have now grown through 
4 operating projects in FY '26, and we achieved about INR 2,300 crores in sales. In this year, in 
the second quarter, as Lodha mentioned, we have launched a project and are ready to launch 
another project in the second half of this year.  
With this, we would have six operating projects by the end of FY27 and we are likely to cross 
about INR 3,000 crores in pre-sales from Bangalore in this financial year. Over this period, we've 
also established presence across key group corridor for Bangalore and as we have scaled our 
strategic focus; has remained consistent; build, premium and luxury developments in locations 
where we believe the depth of end user demand; and to differentiate ourselves through the 
quality of our product and customer experience.  
I would like to talk a little about the launch of Lodha Beaumont Estate, as Mr. Lodha mentioned, 
the significant milestones in this year for us. This is a 70-acre development in North Bangalore. 
We have reported sales of about INR 1,500 crores plus in the first 3 months since launch. 
Response to Beaumont estate has been particularly encouraging for us for a few reasons.  
First, the product differentiation. We introduced large-format premium homes in a micro 
market where much of the existing supply was at a relatively smaller typologies and lower 
ticket sizes. Beaumont estate were priced above INR 3 crores with a few units going up to as 
high as INR 13 crores to INR 14 crores compared to the fact that most of the competition supply 
was at around INR 2 crores. Importantly, larger premium homes have much greater demand 
by our customers.  
Second, the premium lifestyle proposition. The project has been designed as a premium garden 
estate with a strong emphasis on open spaces, landscaping and high-quality amenities, 
including a large signature club house. We believe this differentiates proposition has related 
strongly with customers in the macro market. 
 
Third, an expensive customer experience. As we have done in our previous projects in 
Bangalore, we place significant emphasis on the quality of customer journey at Beaumont 
estate. It included a pointed customer engagement, consultative sales and high hospitality 
standards including curated F&B experiences. We believe the customer experience during the 
purchase journey gives buyers an early indication of the service standards and leading 
experience we aim to provide after possession as well.  
Fourthly and most importantly, the success also allays some concerns over AI-led job 
disruptions in Bangalore. The disruption, we believe, is more a phenomenon at the entry-level 
jobs, which pays around INR 500,000 to INR 600,000 per annum salaries, a segment which is 
not our customers. Most of our target segments in this project are those who have household 
income of above INR 50 lakhs and are probably net gainers of the AI net productivity gains and 
are actually very, very confident cohort.  

 
 
 
8 
 
The success of Beaumont estate gives us further confidence in the premium positioning that 
we've been building in Bangalore over the last few years. More importantly, the depth of 
demand across ticket sizes, including at the upper end of the project, reinforces I believe that 
there is a meaningful and growing customer base for differentiated premium and luxury 
housing in the city of Bangalore. 
 
Looking over the past few years, we have re-established Lodha as an aspirational premium 
development in Bangalore and Beaumont estate launch reflects this. As we scale, we will keep 
our focus on premium luxury projects and on delivering exemplary customer experience and 
product across all our projects. 
 
We continue to actively evaluate land parcels, which align with these criteria, build a healthy 
project pipeline. The high growth North-east and South-east Bangalore corridors remain a 
priority, and we continue to explore opportunities closer to the city as well. Over the longer 
period, we want to become a meaningful player in the city and see ourselves having a mid-teen 
market share. 
 
From a people's point, we have scaled significantly from starting up in 2023 to about 350 plus 
employees across all functions. We expect this number to grow significantly over the next year, 
especially in operations, in line with our growth ambitions. As always, we will continue to 
leverage support from our head office, which has a strong employee base who support us in 
every functions, while depending on a strong core team in Bangalore to lead and deliver. Thank 
you. 
Abhishek Lodha: 
We can open the floor for Q&A. 
Moderator: 
Sure, sir. Thank you very much. We will now begin with the question-and-answer session. We 
will take the first question from the line of Karan Khanna from Ambit Capital. 
Karan Khanna: 
Congrats on the strong operating profit growth for the quarter and also the Bangalore success. 
My first question to you, Abhishek, and while you did briefly talk about this during your opening 
remarks. We've had two quarters since the start of the West Asia war. Based on the trends that 
you're seeing, which segment has been impacted the most in terms of footfalls because of the 
crisis?  
And as a follow-up for your portfolio, South and Central Mumbai accounted for about INR 8,000 
crores of sales in FY '26. So how is the luxury segment trending overall since the start of the 
war and of the 5.6 million sq. ft slated for launch in MMR, what's the share of South and Central 
in the launch pipeline? 
 
 

 
 
 
9 
 
Abhishek Lodha: 
Karan, thank you for your questions. In terms of the impact on the footfall from the Gulf war, 
as I mentioned in my opening remarks, the only impact we've seen so far in terms of sales is 
from the NRI sales in the Middle East, which make up about 4% to 5% of our sales. And these 
tend to be more focused entry level, which are homes between INR 1 crores to INR 3 crores.  
So that's where sort of the impact has been seen. We haven't seen any other meaningful 
change in terms of our footfalls on account of the Middle East situation. In terms of the strength 
of the market in a Central Mumbai or what you refer to as a luxury buyer, we continue to see 
strong demand. We see that the consumer for that segment is constructive.  
They're making their sales decisions. And they are clearly differentiating between the options 
that they have on the basis of the credibility of the brand and the location. So, we find that all 
these factors are supportive of our continued scale up in this segment. In terms of the launch 
pipeline, we have about INR 100 billion GDV in the MMR of which about South-Central Mumbai 
launches will be approximately INR 40 billion. 
Karan Khanna: 
Sure. This is helpful, Abhishek. Secondly, can you talk a bit about the office opportunity in NCR, 
while it is too early, how is the initial response for your commercial project that was launched 
on Golf Course Road? And is this part of the strategy for NCR where you build brand visibility 
with commercial followed by our Q4 launch at Sohna Road? As a follow-up, when you're 
looking at future opportunities, are you evaluating both commercial as well as residential or 
will the focus largely remain on adding more residential projects in this region? 
Abhishek Lodha: 
Development business focuses on for sale product across office as well as residential with 
residential obviously being by far the dominant component of that strategy. In terms of the 
launch that we've recently started this festive season in NCR. The response so far has been 
quite encouraging. Obviously, these are early days. So, we will have a more detailed update for 
you in the next quarter's analyst call. 
 
In terms of our strategy, whether again, residential or office in the NCR. NCR, as you know, we 
are in pilot phase. We will do a very modest number of projects in the early days. And we have 
currently this launch project, 1 more, which we have visibility of, and we'll perhaps add a third 
site soon and then take it from there. So, as it stands right now, this is the first of our office 
projects, and we expect to have 2 more residential projects in our pilot phase and then 
evaluate. 
Karan Khanna: 
Sure. And then last question, if I look at Slides 14 and 15, the launch guidance for FY '27 in July 
was about INR 25,000 crores, but now that stands reduced to INR 23,100 crores and yet you 
maintained the pre-sales guidance of INR 24,000 crores. So, is it safe to assume that sustaining 
sales should continue remaining stronger?  
 

 
 
 
10 
 
And as a follow-up, while sustaining sales have been very strong this quarter as well as in first 
half. How should one think about the sustenance sales from completed unsold inventory? If I 
look at Slide 17 of the presentation and the number 3.9 million square feet on completed 
unsold inventory, that remains unchanged this quarter versus last quarter. So, are you seeing 
a trend where completed inventory is still taking longer to sell versus launched, but have we 
completed the inventory? 
Abhishek Lodha: 
Karan, I think that question on completed inventory, almost no completed inventory actually 
stays. Completed inventory is the fastest moving when you imagine that we have deliveries of 
10 million, 11 million, 12 million square feet depending on the year. We will obviously have 
each quarter a significant amount completing and that gets added.  
It's just a coincidence that last quarter and this quarter, the math has just added up to 3.9 
million. It's not the same 3.9 million feet, which is remaining unsold. And in terms of the launch 
pipeline. See launches move around, there'll always be a month here or on there. It doesn't 
change our outlook.  
You've seen that even in previous years, we never really on a full year basis, been explaining 
the fact that just because the launch moved from 1 year to the start of the next year, that 
should not affect the expectation from us in terms of our delivery on our KPIs. So yes, while 1 
project seems to have moved from Q4 into Q1 of the next fiscal, that doesn't change our 
outlook in terms of our pre-sale’s performance. And it also tells you that overall, the underlying 
momentum is good, which is what really sustainable sales is all about. 
Karan Khanna: 
That is helpful Abhishek. Greetings to you and to the entire team for the festive season. 
Abhishek Lodha: 
Thank you. To you, too.  
Moderator: 
Thank you. Will take the next question from the line of Abhinav Sinha from Jefferies. 
Abhinav Sinha: 
A couple of questions. So firstly, on the data center a bit where you've seen the availability now 
being increased to 5 gigawatts from 3. So, can you talk a bit about what is driving this higher 
visibility? And also, how do you see that transmission and distribution aspect of this panning 
out in the next couple of years? 
Abhishek Lodha: 
Abhinav, in terms of the power, the update is really reflective of the approvals that we've 
received from the concerned authorities. So, we've updated it in line with those approvals. This 
5 gigawatts is an outcome of the available transmission ecosystem in and around the site, and 
it doesn't require a significant upgradation of the existing transmission network. 
 
We obviously are carrying out the tapping of that network by building the substations at our 
own cost, for which work is underway, but that is being done by us at our cost. So, we see that 
with this scale of availability, the fact that we have 3 marquee tenants already building on the 
site, AWS, STT and digital edge.  

 
 
 
11 
 
With these tenants what they are building, a lot of it is getting taken up quite quickly by the 
world's largest companies. And as a whole, there is a good bounce when it comes, like I said, 
to our own progress as well as additional land requirements from existing as well as new 
companies to start within the campus. It's important to note that with this campus of about 5 
gigawatts of input power, which will translate into a little over 4 gigawatts of IT output. 
 
The level of investment that India will get will be in the range of $150 billion or more. And this 
will become 1 of the largest, if not the very largest locations for FDI in the country. So, what 
we're building is not just about 1 more project, but we are building a nationally strategic piece 
of infrastructure, which we think will be critical for India's long-term ambitions and we are 
receiving strong support from the government because they recognize how important this is 
for India's future strength. 
Abhinav Sinha: 
Second question is on pre-sales for the first half of the year. Can you detail a bit on the trends 
that you have seen in Mumbai, which segments or geographies are doing better? 
Abhishek Lodha: 
We Abhinav saw that we ended up with good sales across the different price points. So, there 
isn't anything specifically to report in terms of 1 geography, Mumbai performing stronger or 
weaker than the other? The monsoon quarter typically is quite soft. So, we were very pleased 
with the overall sales for this quarter. Especially, since there was no land contribution to it.  
                                                     The mid-income segment contribution went up modestly in this quarter compared to the last 
quarter. But there's nothing really in terms of a larger trend that we are seeing. Sales across 
the different price points continue to remain quite positive.

Global.

Sir, I missed the part on data center…

audible?

a Impact of new Labour Codes
On November 21, 2025, the Government of India notified provisions of the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social 
Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, ('Labour Codes’) which consolidate twenty-nine existing labour laws 
into a unified framework governing employee benefits during employment and post-employment. The Labour Codes, amongst other things introduces changes, 
including a uniform definition of wages and enhanced benefits relating to gratuity and leave. The Company assessed the financial implications of these changes 
which has resulted in increase in gratuity and leave liability arising out of past service cost by ? 30.42 crores for the year ended March 31, 2026. Considering 
the impact arising out of an enactment of the new legislation is an event of non-recurring nature, the Company has presented this amount as “Impact of new 
Labour Codes" under “Exceptional Item” in the Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended March 31, 2026.
5 At the meeting of the Board of Directors of the Company held on June 26, 2026, it was resolved to amalgamate M/s. Krebs Biochemicals & Industries Ltd. with 
the Company, subject to necessary consents/approvals. The appointed date for this amalgamation is April 1, 2026. However, pending consents/approvals, no 
effect for this amalgamation has been given in the unaudited financial results.
6 The Company has only one operating segment viz. 'Pharmaceuticals'.

Delhivery Limited - Q2FY27 Earnings Conference Call 
October 30, 2026 
  
  
 
 
  
Management: ​
Mr. Sahil Barua, MD and Chief Executive Officer 
                    ​ ​
​
Ms. Vani Venkatesh, Deputy CEO 
                    ​ Mr. Vivek Pabari, Chief Financial Officer 
                    ​ ​
​
Mr. Varun Bakshi, Chief Sales Officer 
                    ​ Mr. Navneet Kumar, Head of Supply Chain Solutions 
  
Moderator: ​ ​
Mr. Dhruv Jain, Ambit Capital
 

Dhruv Jain : Good evening everyone. Welcome to the Q2FY27 earnings call of Delhivery 
Limited hosted by Ambit Capital. 
  
Before we start, Delhivery would like to point out that some of the statements made in today's 
call may be forward looking in nature and a disclaimer to this effect has been included in the 
earnings presentation shared with you earlier. Kindly note that this call is meant for investors and 
analysts only. If there are representatives from the media, they are requested to kindly drop off 
this call immediately. 
  
To discuss the result, we are pleased to welcome Mr. Sahil Barua-MD and CEO, Ms. Vani 
Venkatesh-Deputy CEO, Mr. Vivek Babari-Chief Financial Officer, Mr. Varun Bakshi-Chief 
Sales Officer and Mr. Navneet Kumar-Head of Supply Chain Solutions. As a reminder, all 
participants' lines will be in listen mode only and participants can use the hand raise feature to 
ask any questions post the opening remarks. Now, I will invite Mr. Sahil Barua to take us through 
the highlights of the quarter and post which we will open the floor for Q&A. Thanks and over to 
you, Sahil. 
  
Sahil Barua : Good evening, everyone. Thank you for joining us this Friday evening and Dhruv 
and Ambit team, thank you for hosting us this evening. As usual, a quick summary of the quarter 
and then we will jump straight to Q&A. 
  
Broad summary is it has been a very satisfactory quarter. As you are aware, quarter one was a 
slightly challenging quarter with the volatile macro environment. But quarter two has gone more 
or less to plan. 
  
We have had a record quarter in terms of volumes, revenues and overall business profitability. 
Our express business delivered 325 million shipments in Q2FY27. So, we are up about 32% 
YoY. 
  
The PTL business delivered 545K metric tonnes of freight, up about 14.2% YoY. Overall 
revenue from services for the company crossed Rs. 3,000 Cr for the first time at Rs. 3,066 Cr for 
Q2FY27, which is up 20% YoY. Adjusted EBITDA came in at Rs. 123 Cr or 4% of revenue with 
PAT of Rs. 41 Cr. 
  
The company also continues to be extremely well capitalised with Rs. 4,676 Cr of cash on the 
balance sheet. Many of the improvements that we have been driving over several quarters, which 
is in terms of managing capital intensity, improving net working capital position of the business, 
and also some of our sustained investments in new businesses and frontier areas in AI 
engineering and technology are also beginning to play out. We have released most of this 
information as part of our shareholder's letter, which is now publicly available. 
  

So, with that, I will pause here. Our presentation is also up, but happy to take questions as they 
come up. Dhruv, over to you. 
  
Dhruv Jain : Thanks, Sahil. As a reminder, anyone who wishes to ask a question may use the 
raise hand feature and we will put you on.  
 
The first question is from Vijit Jain. Vijit, please go ahead. 
  
Sahil Barua : Hey, Vijit. 
  
Vijit Jain : Hi, can you hear me? 
  
Dhruv Jain : Yes, please go ahead. 
  
Vijit Jain : Yes, sorry. I was just congratulating you, but my question is on Express Parcel. You 
have said before that growth in FY27 would be in the 20-30% range, probably mid, even upper 
end of that. Sitting where you are right now, just wanted to know, are you closer to that upper 
end still? That's my first question. And I then wanted to follow up on a couple of things. 
  
Sahil Barua :  
Vijit, why don't you go through with all your questions and I'll take them all at the same time. 
  
Vijit Jain :  
Yeah, sure. My second question was your investments that you've mentioned here, shifting focus 
on more automation, ASRS, etc. When you compare all of these new investment areas in core 
business to things like 40 feet trucks and automated sorters that you've done before, those 
obviously paid off in pretty significant ways. How does this compare in terms of potential scale?  
 
And then, similarly, on the revenue side, I wanted to understand, if I look at some of these new 
initiatives, same day, next day expansion, Delhivery Direct, and financial services, so on, how 
would you scale them in terms of opportunity that you see in each of these? So, those are my 
questions. 
  
Thank you. 
  
Sahil Barua : Sure. Thanks, Vijit. Let me go through these as quickly as I can. 
  
So, volumes, as you can see, have been growing over 30% YoY. As things stand, the month of 
October has also been a pretty good month for us. And we're ahead of where we actually 
expected to be as of this month. 
  

Now, what's surprising, I had spoken about this in Q1 is that despite a fairly volatile macro 
environment, volumes have broadly held up. And so, as things stand, I don't really see any 
reason for us to revise our estimate of growth. In fact, we are at the moment, beyond the upper 
end of the 20-30% that we had guided at the start of the year. 
  
So, it looks like we should easily be. The worst case should be that we would be at the upper end 
of that. So, I think it's going to turn out to be a reasonable year from a volume standpoint. But 
again, frankly, US midterm elections are on Tuesday. So, let's see how things go.  
 
To your second question, let me answer your third question first, and then come to the second 
one, which was on automation which was a slightly more nuanced question. On the revenue side, 
same day, next day delivery, I've spoken about this in the past, our volumes in this segment are 
actually pretty significant. The only reason we don't disclose or talk about the same day, next 
day, beyond a certain point is because when you compare the same day, next day volumes to the 
overall massive scale that the business has, it doesn't look as large. But suffice to say, our same 
day, next day business is easily north of a couple of hundred crores in overall revenues. What we 
do also is not just the pure transportation of same day, next day services, it's also, in some senses, 
a part of our supply chain services business, because we also provide integrated fulfillment 
solutions to vertical brands. So, it's a pretty meaningful business overall.  
 
But, let me just say, were we to split it out, this business would probably look like a Rs. 300, 400, 
500 Cr business, all things put together. But, we don't disclose it largely because it's 
fundamentally running on the same network and part of a much larger express network. 
  
We will continue to invest in building out more of these fulfilment centres. We have several 
across all of maybe the top 15 major cities. So, continuing to expand that footprint, continuing to 
grow the client base over there is obviously a priority. 
  
Coming to Delhivery Direct, there are two parts of this business. One is Delhivery Local, which 
is our in-city on-demand commercial vehicle renting service. That has actually been a pretty big 
positive surprise. Our aim was to really get to maybe Rs. 240-250 Cr ARR by exit of this 
financial year. As things stand, we've already crossed Rs. 200 Cr and are growing faster than we 
originally expected. We are also ahead in terms of contribution margin compared to our original 
expectations. Our original expectation was that CM breakeven would happen earliest, maybe 
early to middle part of next financial year. But as things stand, it's looking more like CM 
breakeven could happen as early as Q4 of this financial year. So, I'm hopeful. We're in eight 
cities now. I'm hopeful if things continue that we should cross, even potentially a Rs.270-280 Cr 
run rate on this. How large could this business be? As I mentioned before, it's very hard to say. 
The addressable market for in-city shipping using LCVs is very, very large. There are players in 
this space already. Porter's obviously a good example of a great company in this space. So it does 
feel like the headroom for growth here is massive.  

 
We also do intercity Delhivery Direct, which is also focused on non-e-commerce but express 
parcel shippers. 
  
This business also is now slowly becoming quite material. It's accessed, obviously, through the 
Delhivery Direct application. And for SMEs, they use the Delhivery One application. 
  
These businesses also today are material businesses. Delhivery Direct for consumers today, for 
example, is probably running at close to nearly Rs. 100 Cr, in maybe about 15 months of focused 
effort on the business.  
 
The international business also has picked up. The Saver business that we had launched, are 
today hitting probably close to  Rs. 140 Cr ARR in this business. It's actually grown 55% QoQ 
between Q1FY27 and Q2FY27 and has also broken even at a service EBITDA level. So both of 
these things have been pretty big positive surprises. Addressable market for economy, 
international shipping is pretty large. Our estimation is that over the next three or four year 
period, the economy plus express shipping revenues for Delhivery could end up being a low four 
digit crores. This could be a Rs. 900-1,000 Cr kind of opportunity for us and a profitable one at 
that. 
  
That leads us to financial services. On financial services, I think it's better for me to comment 
once we have all our ducks in a row. A lot of this year has been spent on getting ourselves set up 
regulatorily to be able to expand this business. We're in the business of eventually being able to 
extend, through partners, loans to fleet owners who can then attach their vehicles into the 
Delhivery network. And then launch that for electric vehicles, launch it for LCVs as well, and 
then also offer other financial products like insurance. Monetization has begun, but at this stage, 
it's at a very, very, very early stage. So, we will be in a better position to comment at the end of 
this financial year. 
  
Coming to the second question, which was on automation. Seeing the tractor trailers and the 
sorters, I do want to point one thing out, with the benefit of hindsight now, it feels like a lot of 
the market is looking at our investments in tractor trailers and sorters and saying, these are slam 
dunk investments that paid off. But it would be remiss of me to not point out that at the time that 
we began bringing tractor trailers into India, and similarly, nearly 12 years ago, when we bought 
out practically all of India's sorter capacity, the collective reaction really was that this was an 
investment that didn't make sense. And there was a lot of questioning about whether it would pay 
off at all.  
 
Our view on automation fundamentally now is that it is an existential question, because the 
reality is the labour environment in India has been steadily becoming more volatile and more 
challenging. 

  
One of the reasons, obviously, is labour availability has been challenging. Seasonal fluctuations 
in labour availability are pretty large. The second issue is regulation for the workforce has 
changed quite a lot. And it's quite volatile overall, minimum wages keep getting revised. There's 
a whole bunch of compliance that keeps changing. And staying abreast of that obviously is 
challenging. And the third reality is that the impact of climate on labour availability and 
workforce productivity is pretty significant. 
  
When we do the math, our view is that Indian labour when adjusted for productivity is 
increasingly becoming uncompetitive. And therefore, as a consequence, the investment in 
automation is beginning to look better and better and better. The other advantage, of course, is 
the price of automation is coming down. 
  
And, as people who've invested in this space for a very long period of time, we are also 40% 
shareholders in Falcon Autotech, we understand how the cost curve for automation works. And 
we do believe we're at that cost in terms of new robotic systems that we otherwise would simply 
have been unable to deploy maybe three or four years ago. 
  
We have spoken about both self-developed autonomously guided vehicles for in-facility 
movements. But we've also begun to pilot and experiment with other interesting robotic systems 
across our mid-mile operations. So my sense is that the paybacks will easily match the payback 
periods that we've seen in the past for TTs and for sorter systems. 
  
On the software front, because that's also been one area where investments have been. We've 
spoken about this in the last four quarters, we have been spending on AI initiatives within the 
company. Four quarters back, a lot of this was really focused around the software development 
life cycle. It really was about how we make our own technology teams more productive. But, 
today with four quarters of work behind us, we are beginning to finally see fairly material 
improvements in service and cost outcomes through our AI initiatives, whether it's a combination 
of reducing claims, which is one of the more obvious use cases, or one of the less obvious ones, 
but that has worked out is improving sales productivity, through auto generating bids. The other 
one, has been Delhivery Maps , which over the last two quarters, the sophistication it has reached 
is already saving us a million dollars a year, compared to using Google APIs. 
  
So, these initiatives are going to pay off even faster. And so when you look at our overall 
investments in engineering and technology, one, these are existential and essential for any 
company that's serious about scaling, and, second, they will pay off exactly as fast, if not faster 
than the TTs and the sorters. 
  
Vijit Jain : Got it. Thank you so much, Sahil, for that answer. Just wanted to check, one question 
that comes up is you guys have what are known as unbilled receivables, right? And I know those 

numbers have been coming off, your working capital improvement has been pretty sharp. But in 
general, because you mentioned something along the lines of that in the letter, do you see more 
meaningful improvement there from these AI initiatives as well, ability to kind of bring your 
unbilled receivables and the like to kind of zero? 
That was my last question. 
  
Vivek Pabari : Automation will certainly help in further improving our collection cycle because 
faster billing, more accurate billing and faster claim resolution, AI driven automation will help in 
all of these things and hence our receivables can further improve. But unbilled will not have 
anything to do with it. Unbilled is more of an accounting concept where a shipment which is not 
completed it's a life cycle in the network, a partial revenue has to be accrued as per accounting 
rules and hence it shows up in unbilled. So it's more of an accounting construct, I would say, and 
wouldn't have anything to do with AI. 
  
But in general, AI certainly helps us further compress our working capital cycle. 
  
Vijit Jain : Got it. Thank you. Those were my questions. 
  
Dhruv Jain : Thanks, Vijit. The next question is from Gaurav Rateria. Gaurav, please go ahead. 
  
Gaurav Rateria : Hi. I hope I'm audible. 
  
Sahil Barua : Yes, you are. 
  
Gaurav Rateria : Yeah. Hi. Congrats, Sahil, on good execution on margins. 
  
I have two or three questions. First, I see a lot of focus in the shareholders letter around visibility 
to get to the margins that we desire in different matured business segments that we have. I'm just 
curious that is it kind of hurting our market share aspirations in the core segments like Express? 
Because I see that the volume growth turned out to be slightly muted in the current quarter. 
That's question number one.  
 
Question number two is, I understand the cost that impacted us and then we are catching up on 
those and margins are improving and you gave a visibility of H2FY27. 
  
But let's say on a full year basis, in a year where we have seen excellent volume growth in the 
industry and for us as well, we have gained market share. Is it fair to say that we should still be 
on a full year basis expanding margins compared to last year?  
 
And the last question is that you did outlay a couple of initiatives in the core Express segment to

fructify and help on your volume growth aspirations, mostly coming in the numbers in FY28? 
Yeah, these are the three questions. Thank you. 
  
Sahil Barua : Yeah, sure. Let me go again one by one. Your first question was around Express

One of the things that we've spoken about in the past is that yes, of course, our sensitivity to 
profitability is significant because our belief is and you've seen this in the past, I've spoken about 
it, we made an acquisition of Ecom Express, because we do believe that ultimately, profitability 
is more important. And therefore, the selection of volumes that enter your network is actually 
pretty important. And I think I've spoken about this publicly in the past, the way our Express 
network is designed, is fundamentally first to protect the volumes and the service quality of 
everybody who's not a major marketplace. 
  
And only after that, we start looking at the capacities that we have and begin to allocate them. 
And within that, our demand shipping tools are today, very, very sophisticated. And they have 
the ability to both margin manage the volumes that enter our network, but also service manage 
the volumes that enter our network, which means that we do not deem all volumes from all kinds 
of customers to be equal. 
  
To give you one example, if we see a consignment, it doesn't have to be from any specific client, 
it could be an individual shipper, it could be, the largest marketplace in the country, or anyone in 
between, if we see that this is a shipment, which is unlikely to be delivered, or for which we 
believe that we would not be able to provide a reliable service outcome, our systems will 
ultimately prevent manifestation of such products within the network. 
  
One of the things that we see is that during the peak periods or in the build up to the peak 
periods, obviously, some of these controls tend to be a little more loose or a little more fluid at 
shipper end. And so it's important for us as a carrier to be more careful at these moments. So that 
is, of course, a choice that we make. 
 
But just to be clear, it is not a choice that we make purely basis margin, it is also something that 
is service optimised. The other thing that we don't do, obviously, is in these peak periods in the 
absence of demand shaping, which we used to have, maybe three or four years ago, what would 
happen is that if we allowed volumes to come into our network in a fairly random and unfettered 
fashion, all clients would suffer as a consequence of volume surges from specific clients in 
specific areas. And our PTL network would also suffer as a consequence of the same thing. 
 
So our systems are designed to first and foremost safeguard reliability. They are also designed to 
safeguard customer outcomes, and then they are there to safeguard margins as well. So yes, to a 

certain extent, we do demand management, because we don't believe that all volumes are the 
same. 
  
The other thing is to remember is, we don't do as much for example, returns. In this period, our 
absolute volumes of returns, just to be clear, reverse pickups are very substantial. We are in 
absolute volume terms, probably one of the largest players, if not the largest player in this space, 
outside of the self logistics arms, obviously. But that said, our relative share with specific kinds 
of customers may not be as high. And the simple reason is that typically, when you start 
admitting bad quality returns into your network, you will start seeing higher claims. I think you 
can see that our claims ratios, for example, are a fraction of those of the rest of the industry. 
Claims also have a nasty tendency of resulting in revenue provisions or in loss provisions, which 
you have to take in quarters down the line. And we've learned through a lot of experiences, that's 
not something that we want to do. And as a public company, we certainly don't want to do that. 
So we do stay away from that kind of volume.  
 
Your second question was in terms of margin expansion overall. See, I think the absolute margins 
across the transportation network will broadly remain constant. At least that's our outlook for the 
moment compared to where we were last year. So we shouldn't see a degradation of margins in 
the transportation network. Now, that itself, I think, is pretty decent, because we had a rocky start 
to Q1, obviously, with the inflation that we had with fuel. 
  
That said, we've got a number of productivity measures, which are still underway. And if those 
come through, for example, we have certain initiatives which are underway around unitising our 
loads and so on. And the initial results from those experiments have been pretty solid, going 
towards a later end of Q2 and the early part of Q3. 
  
Now, as that continues, and as PTL volumes grow further, that may lead to expansion of margins. 
But rest assured, I think overall transportation margins will broadly be in the range that we said 
they would be in.  
 
And then of course, on SCS, as you can see, margins are normative now that the overall business 
is stabilised. 
  
But I don't know if Vivek has a point of view on this, I'll invite him also. 
  
Vivek Pabari : Yeah, Gaurav, hi, Vivek here. So as Sahil laid out, the overall transportation 
margins, you should see an improvement. PTL has been improving, YoY we will continue that 
journey. 
  
And Express, it should be at least equal to FY26 levels, let me put it that way. But we will 
provide more colour as the year progresses. Because as you know, the third quarter is the key 

quarter for Express. And what happens in the third quarter has a significant impact on the full 
year profitability. 
  
Gaurav Rateria : Thank you, all the best. 
  
Dhruv Jain : Thanks, Gaurav. The next question is from Abhishek Banerjee. Abhishek, you may 
go ahead. 
  
Abhisek Banerjee : Hi, first question, Sahil. Look, we are obviously talking consolidated

Sahil Barua : Sorry, do you mean the service EBITDA for the Express business, the typical

Abhisek Banerjee : Yes. 
  
Sahil Barua : Yeah, so Q3, obviously, is a quarter in which the margins expand quite a lot. And

Abhisek Banerjee : Yes, yes, exactly. And one more clarification. Basically, we wanted to

Sahil Barua : See, on the D2C business, when we look at it across all sizes of customers, which

Somebody will say Nykaa is a D2C company, somebody will say it's not a D2C company, it's a

Sorry, was there a second part to your question as well, right? 

Abhisek Banerjee : That was on the entire 3PL market. 
  
Sahil Barua : On the entire 3PL market, I think if you look at forward logistics, now the entire

And on the contract logistics piece, it's a market that Delhivery doesn't play in. And it's in some

Abhisek Banerjee : Got it. And just one last question, which is on the intra-city Rapid logistics

You did a pilot, but you have kind of dialled down. Now, would you provide some colour why

Sahil Barua : We haven't dialled down, we merely realised that the right format is actually for it

So there's absolutely no change in our desire to provide SDD, NDD services, whether it is two

So there's no change in strategy, just to be very clear. 
  
Abhisek Banerjee : Understood. Thanks. Those were all my questions. 
 

Dhruv Jain : Thanks, Abhishek. The next question is from Sachin Salgaonkar. Sachin, you can

Sachin Salgaonkar : Thanks, Dhruv. Good day, management. Three sets of questions.

Moderator: ​ ​
Mr. Dhruv Jain, Ambit Capital
 

Dhruv Jain : Good evening everyone. Welcome to the Q2FY27 earnings call of Delhivery 
Limited hosted by Ambit Capital. 
  
Before we start, Delhivery would like to point out that some of the statements made in today's 
call may be forward looking in nature and a disclaimer to this effect has been included in the 
earnings presentation shared with you earlier. Kindly note that this call is meant for investors and 
analysts only. If there are representatives from the media, they are requested to kindly drop off 
this call immediately. 
  
To discuss the result, we are pleased to welcome Mr. Sahil Barua-MD and CEO, Ms. Vani 
Venkatesh-Deputy CEO, Mr. Vivek Babari-Chief Financial Officer, Mr. Varun Bakshi-Chief 
Sales Officer and Mr. Navneet Kumar-Head of Supply Chain Solutions. As a reminder, all 
participants' lines will be in listen mode only and participants can use the hand raise feature to 
ask any questions post the opening remarks. Now, I will invite Mr. Sahil Barua to take us through 
the highlights of the quarter and post which we will open the floor for Q&A. Thanks and over to 
you, Sahil. 
  
Sahil Barua : Good evening, everyone. Thank you for joining us this Friday evening and Dhruv 
and Ambit team, thank you for hosting us this evening. As usual, a quick summary of the quarter 
and then we will jump straight to Q&A. 
  
Broad summary is it has been a very satisfactory quarter. As you are aware, quarter one was a 
slightly challenging quarter with the volatile macro environment. But quarter two has gone more 
or less to plan. 
  
We have had a record quarter in terms of volumes, revenues and overall business profitability. 
Our express business delivered 325 million shipments in Q2FY27. So, we are up about 32% 
YoY. 
  
The PTL business delivered 545K metric tonnes of freight, up about 14.2% YoY. Overall 
revenue from services for the company crossed Rs. 3,000 Cr for the first time at Rs. 3,066 Cr for 
Q2FY27, which is up 20% YoY. Adjusted EBITDA came in at Rs. 123 Cr or 4% of revenue with 
PAT of Rs. 41 Cr. 
  
The company also continues to be extremely well capitalised with Rs. 4,676 Cr of cash on the 
balance sheet. Many of the improvements that we have been driving over several quarters, which 
is in terms of managing capital intensity, improving net working capital position of the business, 
and also some of our sustained investments in new businesses and frontier areas in AI 
engineering and technology are also beginning to play out. We have released most of this 
information as part of our shareholder's letter, which is now publicly available. 
  

So, with that, I will pause here. Our presentation is also up, but happy to take questions as they 
come up. Dhruv, over to you. 
  
Dhruv Jain : Thanks, Sahil. As a reminder, anyone who wishes to ask a question may use the 
raise hand feature and we will put you on.  
 
The first question is from Vijit Jain. Vijit, please go ahead. 
  
Sahil Barua : Hey, Vijit. 
  
Vijit Jain : Hi, can you hear me? 
  
Dhruv Jain : Yes, please go ahead. 
  
Vijit Jain : Yes, sorry. I was just congratulating you, but my question is on Express Parcel. You 
have said before that growth in FY27 would be in the 20-30% range, probably mid, even upper 
end of that. Sitting where you are right now, just wanted to know, are you closer to that upper 
end still? That's my first question. And I then wanted to follow up on a couple of things. 
  
Sahil Barua :  
Vijit, why don't you go through with all your questions and I'll take them all at the same time. 
  
Vijit Jain :  
Yeah, sure. My second question was your investments that you've mentioned here, shifting focus 
on more automation, ASRS, etc. When you compare all of these new investment areas in core 
business to things like 40 feet trucks and automated sorters that you've done before, those 
obviously paid off in pretty significant ways. How does this compare in terms of potential scale?  
 
And then, similarly, on the revenue side, I wanted to understand, if I look at some of these new 
initiatives, same day, next day expansion, Delhivery Direct, and financial services, so on, how 
would you scale them in terms of opportunity that you see in each of these? So, those are my 
questions. 
  
Thank you. 
  
Sahil Barua : Sure. Thanks, Vijit. Let me go through these as quickly as I can. 
  
So, volumes, as you can see, have been growing over 30% YoY. As things stand, the month of 
October has also been a pretty good month for us. And we're ahead of where we actually 
expected to be as of this month. 
  

Now, what's surprising, I had spoken about this in Q1 is that despite a fairly volatile macro 
environment, volumes have broadly held up. And so, as things stand, I don't really see any 
reason for us to revise our estimate of growth. In fact, we are at the moment, beyond the upper 
end of the 20-30% that we had guided at the start of the year. 
  
So, it looks like we should easily be. The worst case should be that we would be at the upper end 
of that. So, I think it's going to turn out to be a reasonable year from a volume standpoint. But 
again, frankly, US midterm elections are on Tuesday. So, let's see how things go.  
 
To your second question, let me answer your third question first, and then come to the second 
one, which was on automation which was a slightly more nuanced question. On the revenue side, 
same day, next day delivery, I've spoken about this in the past, our volumes in this segment are 
actually pretty significant. The only reason we don't disclose or talk about the same day, next 
day, beyond a certain point is because when you compare the same day, next day volumes to the 
overall massive scale that the business has, it doesn't look as large. But suffice to say, our same 
day, next day business is easily north of a couple of hundred crores in overall revenues. What we 
do also is not just the pure transportation of same day, next day services, it's also, in some senses, 
a part of our supply chain services business, because we also provide integrated fulfillment 
solutions to vertical brands. So, it's a pretty meaningful business overall.  
 
But, let me just say, were we to split it out, this business would probably look like a Rs. 300, 400, 
500 Cr business, all things put together. But, we don't disclose it largely because it's 
fundamentally running on the same network and part of a much larger express network. 
  
We will continue to invest in building out more of these fulfilment centres. We have several 
across all of maybe the top 15 major cities. So, continuing to expand that footprint, continuing to 
grow the client base over there is obviously a priority. 
  
Coming to Delhivery Direct, there are two parts of this business. One is Delhivery Local, which 
is our in-city on-demand commercial vehicle renting service. That has actually been a pretty big 
positive surprise. Our aim was to really get to maybe Rs. 240-250 Cr ARR by exit of this 
financial year. As things stand, we've already crossed Rs. 200 Cr and are growing faster than we 
originally expected. We are also ahead in terms of contribution margin compared to our original 
expectations. Our original expectation was that CM breakeven would happen earliest, maybe 
early to middle part of next financial year. But as things stand, it's looking more like CM 
breakeven could happen as early as Q4 of this financial year. So, I'm hopeful. We're in eight 
cities now. I'm hopeful if things continue that we should cross, even potentially a Rs.270-280 Cr 
run rate on this. How large could this business be? As I mentioned before, it's very hard to say. 
The addressable market for in-city shipping using LCVs is very, very large. There are players in 
this space already. Porter's obviously a good example of a great company in this space. So it does 
feel like the headroom for growth here is massive.  

 
We also do intercity Delhivery Direct, which is also focused on non-e-commerce but express 
parcel shippers. 
  
This business also is now slowly becoming quite material. It's accessed, obviously, through the 
Delhivery Direct application. And for SMEs, they use the Delhivery One application. 
  
These businesses also today are material businesses. Delhivery Direct for consumers today, for 
example, is probably running at close to nearly Rs. 100 Cr, in maybe about 15 months of focused 
effort on the business.  
 
The international business also has picked up. The Saver business that we had launched, are 
today hitting probably close to  Rs. 140 Cr ARR in this business. It's actually grown 55% QoQ 
between Q1FY27 and Q2FY27 and has also broken even at a service EBITDA level. So both of 
these things have been pretty big positive surprises. Addressable market for economy, 
international shipping is pretty large. Our estimation is that over the next three or four year 
period, the economy plus express shipping revenues for Delhivery could end up being a low four 
digit crores. This could be a Rs. 900-1,000 Cr kind of opportunity for us and a profitable one at 
that. 
  
That leads us to financial services. On financial services, I think it's better for me to comment 
once we have all our ducks in a row. A lot of this year has been spent on getting ourselves set up 
regulatorily to be able to expand this business. We're in the business of eventually being able to 
extend, through partners, loans to fleet owners who can then attach their vehicles into the 
Delhivery network. And then launch that for electric vehicles, launch it for LCVs as well, and 
then also offer other financial products like insurance. Monetization has begun, but at this stage, 
it's at a very, very, very early stage. So, we will be in a better position to comment at the end of 
this financial year. 
  
Coming to the second question, which was on automation. Seeing the tractor trailers and the 
sorters, I do want to point one thing out, with the benefit of hindsight now, it feels like a lot of 
the market is looking at our investments in tractor trailers and sorters and saying, these are slam 
dunk investments that paid off. But it would be remiss of me to not point out that at the time that 
we began bringing tractor trailers into India, and similarly, nearly 12 years ago, when we bought 
out practically all of India's sorter capacity, the collective reaction really was that this was an 
investment that didn't make sense. And there was a lot of questioning about whether it would pay 
off at all.  
 
Our view on automation fundamentally now is that it is an existential question, because the 
reality is the labour environment in India has been steadily becoming more volatile and more 
challenging. 

  
One of the reasons, obviously, is labour availability has been challenging. Seasonal fluctuations 
in labour availability are pretty large. The second issue is regulation for the workforce has 
changed quite a lot. And it's quite volatile overall, minimum wages keep getting revised. There's 
a whole bunch of compliance that keeps changing. And staying abreast of that obviously is 
challenging. And the third reality is that the impact of climate on labour availability and 
workforce productivity is pretty significant. 
  
When we do the math, our view is that Indian labour when adjusted for productivity is 
increasingly becoming uncompetitive. And therefore, as a consequence, the investment in 
automation is beginning to look better and better and better. The other advantage, of course, is 
the price of automation is coming down. 
  
And, as people who've invested in this space for a very long period of time, we are also 40% 
shareholders in Falcon Autotech, we understand how the cost curve for automation works. And 
we do believe we're at that cost in terms of new robotic systems that we otherwise would simply 
have been unable to deploy maybe three or four years ago. 
  
We have spoken about both self-developed autonomously guided vehicles for in-facility 
movements. But we've also begun to pilot and experiment with other interesting robotic systems 
across our mid-mile operations. So my sense is that the paybacks will easily match the payback 
periods that we've seen in the past for TTs and for sorter systems. 
  
On the software front, because that's also been one area where investments have been. We've 
spoken about this in the last four quarters, we have been spending on AI initiatives within the 
company. Four quarters back, a lot of this was really focused around the software development 
life cycle. It really was about how we make our own technology teams more productive. But, 
today with four quarters of work behind us, we are beginning to finally see fairly material 
improvements in service and cost outcomes through our AI initiatives, whether it's a combination 
of reducing claims, which is one of the more obvious use cases, or one of the less obvious ones, 
but that has worked out is improving sales productivity, through auto generating bids. The other 
one, has been Delhivery Maps , which over the last two quarters, the sophistication it has reached 
is already saving us a million dollars a year, compared to using Google APIs. 
  
So, these initiatives are going to pay off even faster. And so when you look at our overall 
investments in engineering and technology, one, these are existential and essential for any 
company that's serious about scaling, and, second, they will pay off exactly as fast, if not faster 
than the TTs and the sorters. 
  
Vijit Jain : Got it. Thank you so much, Sahil, for that answer. Just wanted to check, one question 
that comes up is you guys have what are known as unbilled receivables, right? And I know those 

numbers have been coming off, your working capital improvement has been pretty sharp. But in 
general, because you mentioned something along the lines of that in the letter, do you see more 
meaningful improvement there from these AI initiatives as well, ability to kind of bring your 
unbilled receivables and the like to kind of zero? 
That was my last question. 
  
Vivek Pabari : Automation will certainly help in further improving our collection cycle because 
faster billing, more accurate billing and faster claim resolution, AI driven automation will help in 
all of these things and hence our receivables can further improve. But unbilled will not have 
anything to do with it. Unbilled is more of an accounting concept where a shipment which is not 
completed it's a life cycle in the network, a partial revenue has to be accrued as per accounting 
rules and hence it shows up in unbilled. So it's more of an accounting construct, I would say, and 
wouldn't have anything to do with AI. 
  
But in general, AI certainly helps us further compress our working capital cycle. 
  
Vijit Jain : Got it. Thank you. Those were my questions. 
  
Dhruv Jain : Thanks, Vijit. The next question is from Gaurav Rateria. Gaurav, please go ahead. 
  
Gaurav Rateria : Hi. I hope I'm audible. 
  
Sahil Barua : Yes, you are. 
  
Gaurav Rateria : Yeah. Hi. Congrats, Sahil, on good execution on margins. 
  
I have two or three questions. First, I see a lot of focus in the shareholders letter around visibility 
to get to the margins that we desire in different matured business segments that we have. I'm just 
curious that is it kind of hurting our market share aspirations in the core segments like Express? 
Because I see that the volume growth turned out to be slightly muted in the current quarter. 
That's question number one.  
 
Question number two is, I understand the cost that impacted us and then we are catching up on 
those and margins are improving and you gave a visibility of H2FY27. 
  
But let's say on a full year basis, in a year where we have seen excellent volume growth in the 
industry and for us as well, we have gained market share. Is it fair to say that we should still be 
on a full year basis expanding margins compared to last year?  
 
And the last question is that you did outlay a couple of initiatives in the core Express segment to 
sustain the growth through the rest of FY27 and beyond. Is it fair to say some of these will 

fructify and help on your volume growth aspirations, mostly coming in the numbers in FY28? 
Yeah, these are the three questions. Thank you. 
  
Sahil Barua : Yeah, sure. Let me go again one by one. Your first question was around Express 
and whether the priority for us has been margins versus growth. 
  
One of the things that we've spoken about in the past is that yes, of course, our sensitivity to 
profitability is significant because our belief is and you've seen this in the past, I've spoken about 
it, we made an acquisition of Ecom Express, because we do believe that ultimately, profitability 
is more important. And therefore, the selection of volumes that enter your network is actually 
pretty important. And I think I've spoken about this publicly in the past, the way our Express 
network is designed, is fundamentally first to protect the volumes and the service quality of 
everybody who's not a major marketplace. 
  
And only after that, we start looking at the capacities that we have and begin to allocate them. 
And within that, our demand shipping tools are today, very, very sophisticated. And they have 
the ability to both margin manage the volumes that enter our network, but also service manage 
the volumes that enter our network, which means that we do not deem all volumes from all kinds 
of customers to be equal. 
  
To give you one example, if we see a consignment, it doesn't have to be from any specific client, 
it could be an individual shipper, it could be, the largest marketplace in the country, or anyone in 
between, if we see that this is a shipment, which is unlikely to be delivered, or for which we 
believe that we would not be able to provide a reliable service outcome, our systems will 
ultimately prevent manifestation of such products within the network. 
  
One of the things that we see is that during the peak periods or in the build up to the peak 
periods, obviously, some of these controls tend to be a little more loose or a little more fluid at 
shipper end. And so it's important for us as a carrier to be more careful at these moments. So that 
is, of course, a choice that we make. 
 
But just to be clear, it is not a choice that we make purely basis margin, it is also something that 
is service optimised. The other thing that we don't do, obviously, is in these peak periods in the 
absence of demand shaping, which we used to have, maybe three or four years ago, what would 
happen is that if we allowed volumes to come into our network in a fairly random and unfettered 
fashion, all clients would suffer as a consequence of volume surges from specific clients in 
specific areas. And our PTL network would also suffer as a consequence of the same thing. 
 
So our systems are designed to first and foremost safeguard reliability. They are also designed to 
safeguard customer outcomes, and then they are there to safeguard margins as well. So yes, to a 

certain extent, we do demand management, because we don't believe that all volumes are the 
same. 
  
The other thing is to remember is, we don't do as much for example, returns. In this period, our 
absolute volumes of returns, just to be clear, reverse pickups are very substantial. We are in 
absolute volume terms, probably one of the largest players, if not the largest player in this space, 
outside of the self logistics arms, obviously. But that said, our relative share with specific kinds 
of customers may not be as high. And the simple reason is that typically, when you start 
admitting bad quality returns into your network, you will start seeing higher claims. I think you 
can see that our claims ratios, for example, are a fraction of those of the rest of the industry. 
Claims also have a nasty tendency of resulting in revenue provisions or in loss provisions, which 
you have to take in quarters down the line. And we've learned through a lot of experiences, that's 
not something that we want to do. And as a public company, we certainly don't want to do that. 
So we do stay away from that kind of volume.  
 
Your second question was in terms of margin expansion overall. See, I think the absolute margins 
across the transportation network will broadly remain constant. At least that's our outlook for the 
moment compared to where we were last year. So we shouldn't see a degradation of margins in 
the transportation network. Now, that itself, I think, is pretty decent, because we had a rocky start 
to Q1, obviously, with the inflation that we had with fuel. 
  
That said, we've got a number of productivity measures, which are still underway. And if those 
come through, for example, we have certain initiatives which are underway around unitising our 
loads and so on. And the initial results from those experiments have been pretty solid, going 
towards a later end of Q2 and the early part of Q3. 
  
Now, as that continues, and as PTL volumes grow further, that may lead to expansion of margins. 
But rest assured, I think overall transportation margins will broadly be in the range that we said 
they would be in.  
 
And then of course, on SCS, as you can see, margins are normative now that the overall business 
is stabilised. 
  
But I don't know if Vivek has a point of view on this, I'll invite him also. 
  
Vivek Pabari : Yeah, Gaurav, hi, Vivek here. So as Sahil laid out, the overall transportation 
margins, you should see an improvement. PTL has been improving, YoY we will continue that 
journey. 
  
And Express, it should be at least equal to FY26 levels, let me put it that way. But we will 
provide more colour as the year progresses. Because as you know, the third quarter is the key 

quarter for Express. And what happens in the third quarter has a significant impact on the full 
year profitability. 
  
Gaurav Rateria : Thank you, all the best. 
  
Dhruv Jain : Thanks, Gaurav. The next question is from Abhishek Banerjee. Abhishek, you may 
go ahead. 
  
Abhisek Banerjee : Hi, first question, Sahil. Look, we are obviously talking consolidated 
margins. But if we look at service level, right, you would be nearing the higher end of the band

Sahil Barua : Sorry, do you mean the service EBITDA for the Express business, the typical 
range that we provide, which is the 16-18% range? 
  
Abhisek Banerjee : Yes. 
  
Sahil Barua : Yeah, so Q3, obviously, is a quarter in which the margins expand quite a lot. And

Abhisek Banerjee : Yes, yes, exactly. And one more clarification. Basically, we wanted to

Sahil Barua : See, on the D2C business, when we look at it across all sizes of customers, which

Somebody will say Nykaa is a D2C company, somebody will say it's not a D2C company, it's a

growth across that entire segment has remained as robust as its always been. No major change at 
all. 
  
Sorry, was there a second part to your question as well, right? 

Abhisek Banerjee : That was on the entire 3PL market. 
  
Sahil Barua : On the entire 3PL market, I think if you look at forward logistics, now the entire 
3PL market itself, there's a combination of things. There's the forward logistics piece, there is the 
reverse logistics piece. And I'm deliberately leaving out certain things from this, which is, for

But when you look at the forward logistics space overall, and we look at our volumes on forward

And on the contract logistics piece, it's a market that Delhivery doesn't play in. And it's in some

Abhisek Banerjee : Got it. And just one last question, which is on the intra-city Rapid logistics 
piece. Now, my understanding is you have kind of dialled down on that, right? 
  
You did a pilot, but you have kind of dialled down. Now, would you provide some colour why 
you made that choice? 
  
Sahil Barua : We haven't dialled down, we merely realised that the right format is actually for it

massive base, not as material, but it is still a large enough business. 
  
So there's absolutely no change in our desire to provide SDD, NDD services, whether it is two 
hour delivery, four hour, eight hour or twelve  hour. The only advantage that we found with the
